Chapter 3: The Power of Candor and the 20-70-10 Approach
You know, in a big company, it’s all too common for people to tiptoe around tough topics—hiding behind polite words and avoiding those honest, sometimes uncomfortable conversations. But here’s the thing: real progress? It only happens when people are truly open—with themselves and with each other.
That simple truth became the backbone of a bold management philosophy, one that would end up shaping the company’s future in ways nobody could’ve imagined.
The idea was actually pretty radical. What if candor wasn’t the rare exception, but the everyday norm? Imagine walking into a meeting where everyone’s encouraged to say what they actually think—even if it means disagreeing with the boss or challenging a popular idea.
This wasn’t about being rude or tearing people down. It was about building a space where the best ideas could rise to the top, no matter where they came from.
Over time, those walls of politeness and fear started to crumble. In their place, you got honest debates and real, constructive feedback. And you could feel the energy shift—suddenly, people weren’t just going along to get along. They were pushing each other, questioning assumptions, and working together to find the best solutions.
Now, let’s talk about one of the most talked-about changes: the 20-70-10 rule. It’s pretty straightforward. In any group, about twenty percent are your top performers, seventy percent are solid contributors, and the last ten percent just aren’t meeting the mark.
The real challenge? Reward the top twenty, help the middle seventy get better, and make some tough calls about the bottom ten.
Of course, putting this into practice wasn’t exactly easy. A lot of managers felt uneasy ranking their teams. They worried it might stir up resentment or hurt morale. But let’s be honest—if you treat everyone the same, no matter how they perform, what’s left? Usually, it’s mediocrity and frustration.
This new system forced managers to have those honest, sometimes tough conversations. They had to celebrate wins and address weaknesses head-on, instead of sweeping things under the rug.
And you could see the difference almost right away. High performers felt recognized and motivated—they wanted to keep raising the bar. The folks in the middle suddenly had a clear path to get better, with real feedback and support to help them grow. And yeah, letting people go is never easy, but when it happened, it was done with respect and transparency.
Over time, the whole organization got sharper, more focused, and way more driven.
But here’s what’s really important: this approach wasn’t just about numbers or rankings. It was about building a true meritocracy—a place where effort and results mattered more than who’d been around the longest, or who knew the right people.
The message was clear. Everybody’s got a role to play, but excellence is what’s expected—and what’s rewarded. When people know exactly where they stand and what’s expected of them, most will step up to the challenge.
